claims.text: Helm is a graduated Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) project.

Helm charts are directories of templated YAML manifests, a `values.yaml` file of default inputs, and metadata; the `helm` CLI renders chart templates using Go template syntax and either installs the resulting manifests into a cluster as a release or prints them to stdout.
Helm charts are distributed through Helm repositories and indexed publicly on Artifact Hub.
Helm is open source under the Apache License 2.0 and the Helm project does not ship a commercial tier.
Pulumi is open source under the Apache License 2.0.
Pulumi derives resource ordering from the dependency graph: each resource waits for its dependencies to become ready, and independent resources deploy in parallel.

Helm installs resources in a fixed order by Kubernetes kind (defined in helm/helm pkg/release/v1/util/kind_sorter.go); chart authors cannot declare dependencies between resources or subcharts, except through hook weights.
Helm does not let a chart author declare that one resource depends on another.

The Helm docs state that "the Kubernetes objects from the charts and all its dependencies are aggregated into a single set; then sorted by type followed by name; and then created/updated in that order."

Helm's install order is a hardcoded list of Kubernetes kinds in the Helm source, beginning with PriorityClasses and Namespaces, then Secrets and ConfigMaps, then CustomResourceDefinitions and RBAC, then Services and workloads, with any kind not on the list (including custom resources) last.
Helm uninstall runs the same kind-ordering list in reverse.
Helm sends the sorted manifests to the API server in a single pass and does not wait for one resource to become ready before applying the next.

Helm chart dependencies are a packaging mechanism only: a subchart's objects are merged into the parent chart's set and sorted by kind along with everything else, so a chart cannot express installing one subchart before another or starting a Deployment after a Job completes.
Helm chart hooks can be ordered with `helm.sh/hook-weight` annotations, and resources created by hooks are not managed by Helm as part of the release.
Native sequencing for resources and subcharts has been proposed in HIP-0025, which is still a draft.
In Pulumi, passing one resource's output into another, or setting the `dependsOn` resource option, creates an edge in the dependency graph.
The Pulumi Kubernetes provider waits for each resource to become ready before creating the resources that depend on it, and deploys independent resources in parallel.
Pulumi updates are faster than a strict serial sequence because independent resources deploy in parallel.
Pulumi deletes follow the dependency graph in reverse.

The Pulumi Kubernetes `helm.v4.Chart` resource supports the `config.kubernetes.io/depends-on` annotation for ordering between objects inside the chart, and `dependsOn` on the chart for dependencies on resources outside it.
Pulumi creates and deletes resources in dependency order, with each resource ready before the ones that depend on it, rather than in a fixed order by kind.

Helm merges the objects from a chart and all of its dependencies into a single set, sorts them by Kubernetes kind, and applies them in that order, so declaring a subchart as a dependency does not make it install first; ordering within a release requires chart hooks with hook weights or application logic.
Pulumi supports general-purpose languages, plus YAML and HCL, for authoring.

Pulumi's Automation API is a programmatic SDK in every supported language for embedding `up`, `preview`, and `destroy` in a host application; the Helm SDK is available in Go only, and other languages must shell out to the `helm` CLI.

Pulumi Policies is open source, with rules in Python, TypeScript, or Open Policy Agent Rego; Pulumi Cloud adds centralized policy management, and the Enterprise edition adds Pulumi-maintained policy packs for CIS, PCI DSS, HITRUST, and NIST.
Helm has no native policy engine; policy is typically delegated to Kubernetes admission controllers such as Kyverno or OPA Gatekeeper.
Helm records each install or upgrade as a numbered release revision, and `helm rollback` restores a prior revision.
A failed Pulumi update leaves the stack partially updated, and users roll forward by reverting program code and running `pulumi up`.
Helm favors fast revision-based rollback of a single release; Pulumi favors scriptable control over resources from many providers in one update.
Helm and Pulumi are commonly used in combination rather than as substitutes, and two patterns cover most production deployments.

A single Pulumi program can create the cluster (EKS, AKS, or GKE), configure networking and IAM, and install cert-manager, ingress-nginx, and external-dns through `helm.v4.Chart` or `helm.v3.Release`.
The EKS guide at /docs/iac/guides/clouds/aws/eks/ walks through the pattern of creating a cluster and installing the operational stack via Helm charts end-to-end.

Pulumi resolves chart `values` (including outputs such as an `aws.rds.Instance` connection string, KMS key ARN, managed Redis endpoint, or Cloudflare zone ID) at deploy time and orders the chart install after the resources it depends on.
The FAQ entry "What's the difference between `helm.Chart` and `helm.Release`?" exists on the page as the anchor target.
Using Helm charts directly from a Pulumi program via `helm.v4.Chart` or `helm.v3.Release` is the most common adoption pattern for adopting Pulumi alongside Helm.
Charts can be converted to native Pulumi code by rendering them with `helm template` and converting the YAML with `pulumi convert --from kubernetes`.
`pulumi import` and the `import` resource option import existing in-cluster resources and generate the corresponding code.

The Pulumi Kubernetes provider exposes Helm charts as first-class resources through `helm.v4.Chart` and `helm.v3.Release`, and a Pulumi program can pull charts from any Helm repository (public or private) and pass values as typed Pulumi inputs including outputs from other resources.

`helm.v4.Chart` renders chart templates locally and registers each Kubernetes object the chart produces as an individual Pulumi resource, so every child shows up in plan output, drift detection, and state.
`helm.v3.Release` uses the embedded Helm SDK and creates a real Helm release in the cluster, preserving Helm-specific behaviors like chart hooks, post-rendering, and release history.
There are three common ways to adopt Pulumi alongside or in place of Helm, and they can be combined.
The Pulumi Registry includes AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Kubernetes, Datadog, Cloudflare, GitHub, and Auth0 providers.
